system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2149-06-11 18:38:00 to 2149-06-14 15:18:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including morbid obesity, polymyositis, diastolic heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, and long-term anticoagulation presented for evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding. She underwent hysteroscopy, dilation and curettage, cervical biopsy, and Mirena IUD placement as part of her workup and treatment. Due to her multiple comorbidities, she was admitted for overnight observation. She tolerated the procedure well, remained hemodynamically stable, controlled her pain with oral medications, and resumed normal oral intake. Her warfarin was held perioperatively with heparin line flush for thromboprophylaxis and was restarted prior to discharge. She was discharged home the following morning in stable condition with instructions to avoid strenuous activity and follow up with her gynecologist. Biopsy results showed benign endometrial tissue with no evidence of malignancy, though prior Pap findings of atypical glandular cells warranted continued monitoring.
problems: Unspecified disorders of menstruation and other abnormal bleeding from female genital tract
Abnormal glandular Papanicolaou smear of cervix
Body Mass Index 70 and over, adult
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been feeling more tired and short of breath lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been about a week. I’ve been needing oxygen all the time now—used to be just sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your legs were swelling too, right? You increased your water pill for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I bumped my Torsemide to 125mg. It helped a little, but I still feel puffy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And your INR came back very high—7.1. That’s why we’re keeping you in, to watch for bleeding risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. I haven’t changed my warfarin. I take it just like my nurse tells me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. It might be the new batch from a different pharmacy. We’re holding warfarin for now until your INR comes down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a transfusion or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re not actively bleeding. We did see a positive stool test, but you’ve only had one episode. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My PCA saw blood once in my stool. I haven’t seen it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We won’t do a rectal exam unless needed. Your labs show mild anemia, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been more short of breath, even moving to the commode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen requirement went up. But your chest X-ray looks clear—no signs of heart failure or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be my lungs? I have that ILD from my autoimmune disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your inflammatory markers—ESR and CRP are normal. CK is down from before. No sign of a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s making it harder to breathe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We heard some wheezing. You responded well to a breathing treatment. We think it’s reactive airway disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like asthma? I’ve never had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can develop, especially with other lung conditions. We’ll send you home with an albuterol inhaler to use as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my back and muscle pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on Tylenol at home, and it’s helping. We don’t see signs of polymyositis flare, so we’ll keep your current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still thirsty. My mouth is dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mucous membranes are dry. We’ll make sure you’re drinking enough. We’re also checking your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR is down to 5.8 today—trending in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? When can I restart warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait until it’s below 3. Your home nurse will check it again soon, and you’ll restart based on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I used the albuterol last night and it helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That supports our plan. No wheezing this morning. Keep using it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I follow up with my pulmonologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your PCP will coordinate that. We think this is manageable with the inhaler for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 4.7, still high but improving. No signs of bleeding. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any update on the stool test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture showed contamination, not infection. Stool hasn’t been rechecked, but no new bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit stronger today. Less fatigued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your oxygen saturation is 99% on 2 liters. We’re confident you can go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with all your usual medications except warfarin for now. We’re keeping the albuterol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is stable, and you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today with services at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll use the inhaler if I wheeze and wait for the nurse to check my INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or any bleeding. Otherwise, follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including polymyositis, interstitial lung disease, diastolic heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and morbid obesity was admitted for fatigue, increased oxygen requirement, and a supratherapeutic INR of 7.1. She had recently increased her Torsemide for leg swelling and reported one episode of blood in her stool. Evaluation showed no evidence of heart failure exacerbation, infection, or polymyositis flare. Her dyspnea improved with albuterol treatments, leading to a new diagnosis of reactive airway disease. The elevated INR was managed by holding warfarin, with plans to restart when INR dropped below 3. She remained stable, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged home with an albuterol inhaler and home nursing for INR monitoring.
